nameStory: The Tricolored Bumble Bee gets its name from its striking three-color pattern of yellow, orange, and black bands wrapped around its fuzzy body. It's also called the orange-belted bumblebee because of the distinctive orange band that circles its middle like a bright belt.
description: The Tricolored Bumble Bee is a chunky, fuzzy social bee with bold yellow, orange, and black stripes that make it look like it's wearing a colorful sweater. These ground-nesting bees are common throughout New England and are about the size of your thumb. Like other bumble bees, they live in colonies with a queen and many worker sisters who share the duties of foraging, caring for young, and maintaining their underground nest.

idTips.label: Three-color pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive yellow, orange, and black banding - the orange belt across the middle section is the key giveaway that separates this species from other bumble bees

idTips.label: Fuzzy body texture
idTips.description: Covered in dense, soft hair that feels like velvet if you gently touch a resting bee - this fuzz helps them collect pollen and stay warm

idTips.label: Rounded, robust build
idTips.description: Stocky and barrel-shaped with a pleasantly plump appearance, much rounder than the more streamlined honey bees or wasps

idTips.label: Loud buzzing flight
idTips.description: Makes a deep, audible buzz when flying - you can often hear them coming before you see them as they lumber from flower to flower

habitat: You'll find Tricolored Bumble Bees in a variety of New England habitats including gardens, meadows, forest edges, and anywhere with abundant flowers. They nest underground in abandoned rodent burrows or other cavities in well-drained soil. Look for them foraging on raspberry and blackberry bushes, goldenrod, blueberry flowers, and milkweeds.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hibernation and begin establishing new colonies. You might spot a lone, large female searching for a nesting site or feeding on early spring flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when workers are most abundant and visible. Colonies are at full strength with dozens of fuzzy workers busily visiting flowers throughout the day.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males emerge for mating flights. Activity gradually decreases as the colony winds down and only newly mated queens will survive to hibernate.
seasonality.winter: Only mated queens survive the winter, hibernating underground or in protected spaces. No bumble bee activity is visible during New England's cold months.

funFact: Unlike honey bees that die after stinging once, bumble bees can sting multiple times - but they're so gentle that they almost never do unless you accidentally squish one or directly threaten their nest!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bumble bee species, especially the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which lacks the distinctive orange band. Remember: if you see orange in the color pattern, think "tricolored." Yellow jackets and hornets are much more streamlined and lack the fuzzy, teddy bear-like appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bumble" bees, they're actually quite graceful fliers - the name comes from the old English word "humblen" meaning to buzz or hum, referring to their loud flight sound rather than any clumsiness.
compareHints: The orange band is what sets the Tricolored Bumble Bee apart from its many relatives in New England. The Common Eastern Bumble Bee has yellow and black but no orange, while the Brown-belted Bumble Bee has brown instead of bright orange. Most other local bumble bees stick to yellow and black color schemes, making the tricolored pattern quite distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bumble bees, the Common Eastern Bumble Bee is distinguished by its predominantly black coloration with limited yellow banding, unlike the Brown-belted Bumble Bee which has brown fur, or the Tricolored Bumble Bee which sports distinctive white patches.
Among New England's bumble bees, the Brown-belted is most similar to the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but has a duller, more brownish belt versus bright rusty-red.
Among New England's many bumble bee species, the Two-spotted stands out for its clean black and yellow pattern with those diagnostic two spots.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, the Perplexing Bumble Bee has more white hairs on the head and distinctive reddish mandible tips.
Unlike the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which has more irregular yellow patches, the Yellow-banded has clean, complete yellow bands.

Northern Amber Bumble Bees stand out from other New England bumble bees by their uniform golden-yellow body combined with contrasting pale head hairs—most other species have distinct color bands or patterns.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, Half-black Bumble Bees are noticeably smaller and have more defined black banding rather than the Common Eastern's more blended yellow and black pattern.

Among New England's bumble bees, the Golden Northern stands out for its uniform golden-yellow coloration, while most relatives like the Common Eastern Bumble Bee have distinct black and white/yellow banding patterns.
Unlike social bumble bees in its genus, the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee lacks pollen baskets (specialized hairs for carrying pollen) since it doesn't need to provision its own nest.
Unlike other cuckoo bumble bees in New England like the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee, the Yellowish Cuckoo has more muted, golden-yellow tones rather than bright lemon-yellow.
Red-belted bumble bees are much smaller than common eastern bumble bees and lack the solid yellow thorax of many other species.
